body.text: The scheduler is work-conserving: when UDP has less to send than its configured UDP share, TCP receives the unused share, so TCP goodput is nearly independent of weightUdp for weights that keep UDP loss acceptable.
body.question: Does TCP get unused UDP link share?
body.why: It tells which weightUdp values can maximize TCP without hurting UDP.
body.prediction: tcp_goodput_bps at weightUdp=0.40, 0.70, and 0.95 will each be within 1% of tcp_goodput_bps at weightUdp=0.50.
body.observations: E0 default: UDP delivered 300.0032 Mbps with zero loss, TCP delivered 668.633 Mbps, link_util=1.0, drops_band1=92 and tcp_retrans=92. The payload total is 968.6 Mbps, not 1000 Mbps, because link_util counts wire bits including packet overhead and TCP payload is only part of each 1500-byte packet. The most important unexplained behavior is the scheduler when UDP demand is below its configured share: with weightUdp=0.5, TCP already gets about 669 Mbps, close to the link capacity left after UDP wire demand, which suggests TCP may borrow unused UDP share, but this is not stated. A second unknown is the minimum weightUdp that keeps udp_loss_frac <= 0.01; UDP wire demand appears to be roughly 313 Mbps, so weights near 0.30 may underserve UDP.

body.text: UDP loss is controlled by whether UDP's configured link share exceeds UDP's wire demand (about 0.313 of the link); weightUdp=0.30 should lose more than 1% of UDP packets, while weightUdp=0.40 should lose at most 1%.
body.question: At what UDP weight does UDP loss stay under 1%?
body.why: It identifies the safe lower bound for weightUdp.
body.prediction: udp_loss_frac at weightUdp=0.30 will be > 0.01, and udp_loss_frac at weightUdp=0.40 will be <= 0.01.

body.observations: The ledger shows that the default run and every tested feasible weightUdp value from 0.31 to 0.95 give tcp_goodput_bps=668633114 with udp_loss_frac=0.0 (E1, E3). Low-weight runs can raise TCP slightly, but only by dropping UDP: w03005_q100_d2 and w030_q100_d2 have tcp_goodput_bps about 0.86% and 0.93% above default, both inside the 1% tolerance, and both violate udp_loss_frac <= 0.01 (E3). Duration d2 and d30 are equal to default (E2, C5). queuePkts=4 is equal to default, while queuePkts=1000 is about 1.2% lower at default and does not make low-weight UDP loss acceptable (E2, E3). body.limit: The result is limited by the 1Gbps link after satisfying UDP demand under the UDP-loss constraint. At the recommendation link_util=1.0 and UDP is delivered in full at 300003200 bps (E0, E1, E2), so TCP receives only the leftover payload capacity. Dropping UDP to give TCP more is capped by udp_loss_frac <= 0.01: 1% of 300 Mbps is about 3 Mbps, less than 0.5% of TCP goodput, and tested low-weight runs that drop more UDP gain less than 1% and violate the condition (E3, C7).
body.explanation: The default settings achieve the saturated leftover TCP goodput while meeting the UDP-loss condition with zero UDP loss. The scheduler is work-conserving once weightUdp is above UDP demand, so TCP goodput is unchanged from weightUdp=0.31 through 0.95 (E1, C1, V1); weightUdp is kept at the default because it is safely above the UDP-loss threshold, although values below about 0.31 violate the condition (E1, E3, C2, V2). TcpCubic, NewReno, LinuxReno, and Bic all reach the same saturated TCP goodput, while BBR and Vegas are lower because they do not saturate the link (E2, E3, C3, C11, V3). queuePkts=100 is safe: queuePkts=4 is equal but not needed, and queuePkts=1000 can reduce TCP by about 1.2% at default and does not make low-weight UDP loss acceptable (E2, E3, V4). duration does not matter after the one-second warmup (E2, C5, V5). Therefore the default is the simplest setting that reaches the practical maximum TCP goodput under the UDP-loss constraint.
body.holds_when: UDP continues to offer about 300 Mbps, the link remains 1Gbps with MTU 1500, the scheduler remains work-conserving, TCP remains backlogged, and the UDP-loss limit remains 1%.
body.breaks_when: It would change if UDP demand moved the UDP-loss threshold, if the scheduler stopped giving TCP unused UDP share, if TCP were not always backlogged, if the UDP-loss limit were relaxed enough to allow a >1% TCP gain from UDP loss, or if a different queue/variant combination changed link_util.

claims.text: The scheduler is work-conserving: once weightUdp exceeds UDP demand, TCP receives the unused share, so tcp_goodput_bps is unchanged from weightUdp=0.32 to 0.95.
The UDP-loss constraint requires weightUdp of about 0.31 or more at queuePkts=100; weightUdp=0.3005 or 0.30 loses more than 1% of UDP packets.
At the recommendation the link is saturated and UDP is delivered in full, so TCP goodput is the leftover payload capacity.
Loss-based variants (Cubic, NewReno, LinuxReno, Bic) reach the same saturated TCP goodput; BBR and Vegas are lower because they do not saturate the link.
Duration does not materially change measured goodput after the one-second warmup.
Large queuePkts=1000 does not help and can reduce TCP goodput by about 1.2% at default; queuePkts=4 is equal to default.
Lowering weightUdp to steal UDP capacity either violates udp_loss_frac <= 0.01 or gives TCP gains inside the 1% tolerance.
The allowed 1% UDP loss can free at most about 3 Mbps of UDP payload, less than 0.5% of TCP goodput, so it cannot create a >1% TCP gain.

open_questions: The exact weightUdp threshold between 0.3005 and 0.31 was not located.
Whether intermediate queue sizes could make weightUdp near 0.3005 satisfy udp_loss_frac <= 0.01 was not tested.
The exact theoretical maximum TCP goodput under exactly 1% UDP loss was not directly measured, although the bound is below the 1% tolerance.
